articles.title: 'Batting on a trampoline': Daryl Mitchell explains Wellington pitch after New Zealand's collapse against India

articles.body: New Zealand's batting struggles in the second ODI against India were not just about losing wickets but also about dealing with a surface that offered little consistency. Describing the Wellington pitch as being like "batting on a trampoline", Daryl Mitchell admitted that unpredictable bounce and the difficulty of rotating strike made life uncomfortable for the hosts, who were bowled out for just 134 on Saturday.Mitchell, who top-scored with 55 off 104 balls, said the batters were never entirely sure how high the ball would come through, making it difficult to settle into their innings. While New Zealand managed to scrape together a total, the right-hander conceded that they had hoped to put more runs on the board.“It’s pretty challenging out there. Obviously, we’d always like a few more, but yeah, it’s like batting on a trampoline at times. We weren’t quite sure what height the ball was going to come through at. We scraped. We tried to do all we could and hopefully something special with the ball and you never know,” Mitchell told the broadcasters after New Zealand were bowled out.He also highlighted the difficulty of finding gaps and keeping the scoreboard moving, particularly because of the nature of the drop-in surface, which made taking quick singles a challenge.“All of us found it really hard to rotate the strike as well, and especially being, I guess, a drop-in with no pitches either side. It’s really hard, I guess, to drop and run and it just stops. So you add that to the bounce, sometimes, yeah, the only best option was to try and give it a hoe and see what happens,” he added.Despite the challenging conditions, Mitchell said he tried to stick to his strengths and read the Indian bowlers' plans. However, New Zealand struggled to build partnerships, with wickets falling whenever the hosts appeared to be finding some momentum.“Yeah, I guess just trying to stick to your strengths, and for me, it was when I kind of tried to get a read on what they were trying to do. I was trying to maximise that, but yeah, obviously we wanted to keep extending partnerships as well, and that was probably the challenge, because every time we felt like we got a partnership, we’d lost the wicket,” the all-rounder stated.New Zealand's most productive partnership came between Mitchell and Mitchell Santner, who added 59 runs for the sixth wicket after the hosts were reduced to 53/5. Mitchell's resistance helped New Zealand cross the 130-run mark, but the hosts were unable to build on that recovery and finished with 134.Despite the modest total, Mitchell remained hopeful of a turnaround with the ball. He believed early breakthroughs could put India under pressure and give New Zealand a chance to get back into the contest.“Yeah, look, there’s plenty there, first and foremost. Obviously, there’s not the run-rate pressure that we would have liked, but yeah, if we can knock off a couple early, get into the middle order, you never know what can happen,” he said.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.body: India held their nerve in a rain-interrupted, low-scoring thriller to edge past New Zealand by four runs via the Duckworth-Lewis-Stern (DLS) method in the second ODI on Saturday, taking a commanding 2-0 lead in the five-match series. In a contest dominated by the fast bowlers, India's pace attack set up the victory by bowling out the hosts for 134 before Shreyas Iyer and KL Rahul steadied a shaky chase, which was eventually cut short by rain in Wellington.Chasing a revised target, India were struggling at 113/7 when the weather intervened, leaving them 22 runs short of the target. However, they stayed ahead on the DLS par score to seal a hard-fought victory and put themselves in a strong position in the series.Duffy's early strikes, Jamieson puts India under pressureIndia's chase got off to a disastrous start as Jacob Duffy struck with his very first delivery, dismissing Shubman Gill for a golden duck. The right-arm pacer returned in his next over to remove Virat Kohli, leaving the visitors in early trouble.Rohit Sharma attempted to provide some momentum, but New Zealand's seamers continued to apply pressure. Kyle Jamieson delivered a disciplined spell to remove key batters and leave India reeling at 47/4, bringing the hosts firmly back into the contest.With wickets falling at regular intervals, Shreyas Iyer and KL Rahul took responsibility for rebuilding the innings. Iyer scored a valuable 30 off 46 deliveries, helping India recover from their early setbacks.Rahul, meanwhile, remained unbeaten on 26 off 38 balls, striking two fours and two sixes. He held one end together as wickets continued to tumble before rain brought the contest to an early conclusion.India's pace attack dismantles New Zealand for 134Earlier, India's fast bowlers produced a commanding performance to restrict New Zealand to just 134 in 41 overs. The match had been reduced to 47 overs per side following rain, but the hosts struggled to cope with the visitors' pace and accuracy.Auqib Nabi provided India with an early breakthrough, removing openers Tim Seifert and Will Young to put New Zealand on the back foot. The dismissal of Seifert also marked Nabi's maiden international wicket.New Zealand were further pushed into trouble at 53/3 when Gurnoor Brar delivered a double-wicket maiden, dismissing captain Tom Latham and the in-form Glenn Phillips. The twin strikes left the hosts struggling to recover from the early damage.Daryl Mitchell offered some resistance with a patient 55 off 104 balls. He was given a reprieve on 21 when Shubman Gill dropped a straightforward catch at cover, and the right-hander made the most of the opportunity to keep New Zealand's innings moving.Captain Mitchell Santner provided some support with 31 off 38 deliveries, with the pair adding 59 runs for the sixth wicket. However, the lower order failed to build on their contribution as New Zealand were eventually bowled out for 134.Brar was India's standout bowler, finishing with figures of 4/30, while Nabi, Anshul Kamboj and Axar Patel picked up two wickets each.India move 2-0 ahead as series heads to HamiltonThe four-run DLS victory gives India a 2-0 lead in the five-match ODI series, leaving New Zealand with plenty of work to do in the remaining fixtures.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.body: NEW DELHI: India pacer Gurnoor Brar credited the guidance and support of senior players Virat Kohli, Rohit Sharma and Shubman Gill after delivering a match-winning performance in India's narrow four-wicket victory over New Zealand in the rain-affected second ODI. Brar, who picked up a career-best four wickets for 30 runs, played a crucial role in restricting the visitors to just 134 runs in 41 overs.Speaking after receiving the Player of the Match award, Brar explained that his bowling approach was built around discipline, consistency and trusting his abilities. He revealed that the plan was to focus on hitting the right lengths before using his bouncers at the appropriate moments."My plan was simple – to hit my lengths and back my skills. Every day is a learning opportunity, and I want to keep improving and adapting. I was looking to bowl fuller initially and then use the bouncer at the right moment," Brar told the reporters.The young fast bowler also highlighted the importance of backing players, particularly when conditions or performances do not go their way. According to Brar, the Indian team management continued to show confidence in the bowling unit even on flat Indian pitches, encouraging the pacers to trust their skills and bowl with freedom."Backing is very important for every player. There were flat tracks in India, but we were backed there too by the management. They asked me to back my lengths and told me to bowl with freedom," he added.Brar was particularly appreciative of captain Shubman Gill's leadership and his approach towards supporting teammates. He pointed out that Gill does not judge players solely on individual performances and remains focused on getting the best out of the entire group."Shubman Gill backs everyone and doesn't judge them by their performances. He himself has hunger for both himself and the team," Brar said.The pacer also opened up about the difficult experiences he faced during the matches in Guwahati and at Lord's, admitting that those outings were demotivating. However, he viewed them as important learning experiences that helped him understand the demands of international cricket.Brar revealed that he benefited considerably from spending time with senior Indian batters Virat Kohli and Rohit Sharma during open-net sessions. Their advice, along with Gill's inputs, helped him work on different aspects of his bowling and improve his understanding of the game."Matches in Guwahati and Lord's were demotivating, but it was important to learn from those experiences. I had open nets with Virat and Rohit bhai, and they gave me a lot of inputs. Shubman also guided me," he explained.'I learnt a lot from Umesh Yadav paaji': Gurnoor BrarHe further credited his Ranji Trophy experience and the guidance of senior fast bowler Umesh Yadav for helping him develop consistency. Brar revealed that observing Yadav's ability to repeatedly hit the right areas encouraged him to seek advice about maintaining accurate lengths."I also played the Ranji Trophy, and those overs helped me. I learnt a lot from Umesh Yadav paaji. He took a five-wicket haul in the first match, and I observed how consistently he could hit his lengths. I asked him about it, and he gave me a lot of inputs," Brar added.Brar's performance proved decisive in the contest as he dismantled New Zealand's middle order with well-directed short-pitched deliveries. He dismissed Tom Latham and Glenn Phillips in a double-wicket maiden, leaving the visitors struggling at 53 for five.With Auqib Nabi claiming two wickets for 31 runs and Anshul Kamboj returning figures of two for 25, India's young pace attack bundled New Zealand out for 134. The bowlers also delivered an impressive 176 dot balls, putting the opposition under sustained pressure.However, India's chase was far from comfortable. The hosts lost wickets at regular intervals, with Gill, Kohli and Rohit among the early dismissals. At 113 for seven after 26 overs, India were facing a challenging situation when rain interrupted play.KL Rahul remained unbeaten on 26, ensuring India were ahead of the required Duckworth-Lewis-Stern par score of 109 when the match was eventually called off. The four-wicket victory gave India a 2-0 lead in the five-match series, with Brar's breakthrough performance and the team's collective effort emerging as major talking points.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: From run-fest to a spicy feast: A tale of two 113s in Wellington
articles.summary: WELLINGTON: Cricket can surprise you in more ways than one and the nail-biting, low-scoring thriller at the Hnry Stadium on Saturday was a classic example.
articles.body: WELLINGTON: Cricket can surprise you in more ways than one and the nail-biting, low-scoring thriller at the Hnry Stadium on Saturday was a classic example. A week or so ago, in the third T20I, Abhishek Sharma (113) scored more in a run-feast than the rest of the team combined. In the second ODI of the five-match series, India produced 113 runs in a rain-curtailed contest. The difference between the two 113s was that Abhishek fired his off just 38 balls while India struggled against some hostile bowling from Kyle Jamieson & Co.The weather played its tricks and spiced the drop-in surface but the real difference was the intensity with which the hosts hit during the modest run-defence. At the half-way mark, it seemed like a comfortable 135-run chase but one bouncer at a time, the hosts turned it into a proper contest between bat and ball.India played some loose shots, exposing many batters' techniques against sustained fire from both ends.Shubman Gill departed early, Virat Kohli played a loose shot, Rohit Sharma battled but again played a rash shot and then came the final blow when Axar Patel, coming in at No. 5, kept searching for the way out.The Axar callThe match was delicately placed when Rohit was dismissed in the ninth over but the management persisted with Axar rather than sending in a specialist batter like KL Rahul. India have maintained that Axar will be their preferred option to break the right-hander monotony in the batting line-up but sending him ahead of Rahul on a testing pitch was where India missed a trick, raising questions about whether the left-hander is the right choice for that number.The move worked on slow and turning pitches during the Champions Trophy in Dubai and will help when the spinners bowl in tandem, but it felt like a stretch during the second ODI. Axar was peppered with short stuff and he only looked to cut his way out of trouble. He perished playing a similar shot in the series opener, and a similar intention brought curtains down on his struggle in the middle.Even as wickets tumbled and pressure mounted, Rahul rode the bounce, controlled his pulls and looked at ease while others across both teams looked clueless. Briefly, Shreyas Iyer fought fire with fire but another well-directed short delivery resulted in the Indian vice-captain's wicket.It was a similar story in the first innings when Gurnoor Brar and Co. dished out similar treatment to New Zealand and the hosts also looked all at sea in testing conditions.The two innings did make the last international fixture feel like an anomaly. 397 runs were scored in 33.2 overs during that sixathon on October 27 and Iyer's words at the post-match interaction make so much sense after witnessing what we saw today."When Sanju and I, we went to bat, the ball was seaming, and I was like, how did they manage this? It was simply mind-boggling," Iyer said when he was asked about India's assault.The visitors managed 100 runs in five overs and the pair of Abhishek and Vaibhav Sooryavanshi made the New Zealand attack, featuring three bowlers from the ODI line-up, look pedestrian. Mind-boggling indeed!Yes, the weather helped but it also underlines how special Abhishek's 113 was compared to India's poor labour to 113 today.Brief Scores: New Zealand 134/10 in 41 overs (Daryl Mitchell 55, Mitchell Santner 31; Gurnoor Brar 4-30, Anshul Kamboj 2-25) lost to India 113-7 in 26 overs (Shreyas Iyer 30, KL Rahul 26; Jacob Duffy 3-35, Kyle Jamieson 3-35) by 4 runs via DLS method.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: EXCLUSIVE | 'Cricket, outside the NFL, is the largest media property in the world'
articles.summary: New Delhi: The commercial model that transformed cricket into one of the world’s biggest sporting properties is facing a new test.
articles.body: New Delhi: The commercial model that transformed cricket into one of the world’s biggest sporting properties is facing a new test. The BCCI, Indian cricket and the ICC are all confronting a tougher broadcast market, with renewal deals showing signs of stagnation. As the large gains from media rights deals with JioStar become harder to secure, cricket must look beyond the traditional broadcast-led model to find its next phase of growth.That raises bigger questions about the IPL’s global ambitions, the appeal of Indian cricket to international streaming platforms and the scope to build new revenue streams through technology, fan engagement and stadium experiences. What will it take for the IPL to evolve from a hugely successful domestic property into a truly global sports business? And can India translate cricket’s commercial success into a broader sporting economy?In a conversation with TimesofIndia.com, Tony Simpson, Partner and Sports & Entertainment Lead at global management consulting firm Oliver Wyman, shares his perspective on the opportunities and challenges facing the IPL and Indian sport. Simpson is part of the World Economic Forum's push on shaping the global sports economy and consider India as "underdeveloped and with huge potential".Drawing on his work at the intersection of sport, investment and business strategy, he discusses the limits of the current media-rights model, the importance of international reach and why governance, grassroots infrastructure and stronger investment frameworks will be crucial to India's sporting ambitions.Excerpts:Q. How do you see cricket being perceived currently in the global sports economy from a business standpoint?Tony Simpson: Cricket, outside the NFL, is the largest media property in the world. Yet very few people recognise that. When people look at the global sports economy, they tend to think of American sports and football (soccer), while cricket is often placed alongside rugby and other sports.The reason is that cricket is so dominant in India. It has become almost synonymous with Indian sport, and people tend to look at the IPL as the defining property. The IPL has grown enormously, but cricket's next phase of growth will have to come from international markets, not just India.The IPL has grown enormously, but cricket's next phase of growth will have to come from international markets, not just India. Those markets include North America, Europe, Australia and Asia. The IPL is the jewel in the crown because it brings together players from across these regions.Those markets include North America, Europe, Australia and Asia. The IPL is the jewel in the crown because it brings together players from across these regions. It needs to focus on product quality, reach and community-building. That means investing in production, entering the right markets and, in some cases, making the sport available free-to-air rather than chasing short-term revenue.Once it builds a global fanbase, cricket will be in a much stronger position to commercialise its appeal. It is also an extremely data-rich sport, with significant potential in gaming and fan engagement.The challenge, however, is the current governance structure of cricket. There are tensions between leagues and federations, established cricket nations are adjusting to a changing economic order, and the Caribbean faces the challenge of losing athletes to US scholarships because its development pathways are not sufficiently strong.Q. NFL is largely US centered. In the same way, cricket relies significantly on India. How do you grow in such a scenario?Simpson: It is a real tension, but the opportunity lies in exporting the domestic model globally. The Premier League is a good example: its international media rights are worth more than its domestic rights, even though its domestic deal is larger than that of any other European football league.The IPL can follow a similar path, but it needs to become the leading cricket destination globally. That means investing in production quality and entering markets where it can compete with established sports. In Africa, for example, football dominates.Cricket may need to use free-to-air distribution to build an audience in such markets. It also needs grassroots participation. IPL teams should establish academies and camps overseas, send players to engage with local communities and organise exhibition matches outside India.These efforts can bring in new fans and revenue, particularly in mature sports markets where the value of each fan engagement can be considerably higher. The Indian and South Asian diaspora in Europe, North America and Australia also represents a significant opportunity.This is the responsibility of the IPL, not the ICC. The ICC has to grow the game for everyone; the IPL has to build its own international presence.Q. For the Premier League, a huge chunk of the money comes from the broadcasting deal - international broadcasting rather than the domestic broadcasting deal. Whereas for the IPL, the biggest chunk of money comes from the domestic broadcasting deal. So when it comes to growing it, when it comes to learning from the other biggest big sporting leagues, what should the IPL learn from the Premier League?Simpson: Reliance on media rights is really the first phase in the commercial maturity of a sport. The real value for the IPL will come from stadium optimisation, content and community-building. There is a saying: broadcast makes the season, but the stadium, content and community make a business.That means creating better stadium experiences, premium seating and year-round events at venues. Licensing and merchandising also have considerable room to grow. The IPL needs stronger digital engagement and a better understanding of its fans: who they are, what they watch, what they buy and which teams they support.There is also an opportunity to monetise content beyond live matches, creating value for partners and sponsors. But this needs to be supported by grassroots development and academy pathways that bring new audiences into the sport.The IPL should not assume that broadcast revenue alone reflects the full value of the business. Much of its future growth will come from these other areas, which can also attract private equity and investor capital.Q: Why have the likes of Netflix, Amazon, YouTube etc. stayed away from the IPL?Simpson: There are three key reasons. First, cricket is still largely a South Asian sport. The major streaming platforms tend to support properties with a global footprint because that is the audience they are looking to reach.The IPL currently over-indexes in India and under-indexes elsewhere. To change that, it needs a concerted strategy to grow as a global sport. That could mean free-to-air distribution initially, followed by premium content deals with platforms such as Amazon or Netflix.It also needs creative storytelling beyond matchdays. Formula One's *Drive to Survive* is a good example of how content centred on athletes and teams can draw new audiences into a sport. You cannot simply take a sport into a new market and assume people will watch it, however good the product is.That is why the big streaming platforms are not putting the money on the table at present. The IPL is a brilliant asset, but it remains largely a single-market property.Q. But there’s still an opportunity for Netflix India, Amazon Prime India. Get the rights for the Indian market rather than the global package. Especially considering the market has shrunk from three major players to two major players.Simpson: The issue is that these platforms are buying visual real estate. If I am Netflix and I have global rights to the Champions League, NFL, NBA and Formula One, I can distribute those properties across markets.The cost of putting those sports on in India is only a fraction of what it would cost to acquire the IPL, but they still bring in viewers. The IPL, by comparison, is difficult to amplify beyond India.These platforms assess rights globally. If they can acquire several international sports properties for less than the cost of the IPL, that may make better commercial sense.Q. Speaking of bundles, JioStar, which currently has broadcast rights for the ICC, Indian cricket, the IPL, has the capacity to make bundles and sell to the consumer. Is that something that could dissuade the global streaming giants?Simpson: Technology, direct-to-consumer platforms and personalised fan experiences are the next growth phase for sport. In the subcontinent, mobile phones are central to how people communicate and consume content.One challenge for global platforms is that not everyone has access to 5G or unlimited data. Many people still use 2G, 3G and 4G networks, and data consumption can be expensive. Distribution strategies need to reflect those realities.There is an opportunity for India and South Asia to move towards a more personalised model of content distribution, working closely with telecom companies. Rather than simply broadcasting to everyone, platforms could use data to understand individual users and deliver content accordingly.That is where I see considerable potential, and where global platforms may not yet have the scale or distribution model to make their algorithms work effectively in the sports market.Q. If an international investor or a private equity firm wanted to invest in an Indian sport today, which segment would you suggest that they enter besides cricket?Simpson: The first consideration should be whether the sport has a governance structure robust enough to protect the investment. India is attractive because of its young population, energy and sheer size. But the main barrier to quality investment is the risk profile of the asset, particularly its governance.Investors need clarity on board terms and elections, professional management, long-term media deals, fan engagement and venue ownership. They also need confidence that the team and the organisation they are investing in will still be around in 10 years. These are the factors that make a sports asset investable.Football is one area where investors have tried to build a presence. But success depends on everything from federation governance to player pathways. A league cannot rely on importing players to sustain itself. It needs 12-year-old boys and girls who aspire to play for their local teams.Q. A lot of leagues have tried to replicate the IPL. In terms of format, in terms of marketing, but can a one-size fits all approach be possible?Simpson: You cannot simply replicate the IPL. It is a behemoth and the world's most valuable professional cricket league. Other sports need to develop their own grassroots systems and talent pathways.The franchise model also needs genuine market demand. A franchise is worth only what someone is prepared to pay for it. Scarcity is important, too. One reason IPL valuations are so high is that the number of franchises is limited.If someone can set up another franchise in the same sport around the corner the next day, where is the value for an investor? Leagues need governance structures that provide clarity on how many franchises can exist, how the competition will operate and what the long-term investment framework looks like.Q. Sepp Blatter called India a sleeping giant in 2007. 19 years later, we have a huge young population. What's one thing that India needs to get right over the next decade to become a global sporting economy?Simpson: You cannot build a major sports economy without a pipeline of willing athletes. That starts with children wanting to play sport and having access to local tracks, stadiums and pitches in safe environments.You also need qualified coaches and volunteers, as well as investment from cities and governments. Sport has to become a national priority. That would improve health and educational outcomes, but it also needs to become part of the country's culture. This cannot happen in one generation.A report we produced last month found that 49 per cent of under-30s in India are physically inactive by World Health Organisation standards. You cannot have a statistic like that and expect to build a sports-focused economy.The priority over the next decade should be to ensure that every child is within about a mile of a safe place to play a sport they enjoy, with access to coaches and proper facilities. That needs a clear strategic plan and government commitment.Q. Is there an aspect that remains largely unexplored in the Indian sporting ecosystem?Simpson: Women's sport is one of India's biggest opportunities. The Women's World Cup was probably the most-viewed women's sporting event in the world. While cricket competes with American sports and football for attention, women's sport could become one of the biggest sporting properties globally in the near future.South Asia may not fully recognise the scale of this opportunity, but it is a huge asset. Women's sport is empowering and can drive social cohesion in a way few other things can.Women's sport is one of India's biggest opportunities. South Asia may not fully recognise the scale of this opportunity, but it is a huge asset. Women's sport is empowering and can drive social cohesion in a way few other things can.Q. FIFA has their own broadcasting platform. As does the NBA, NFL, NHL, MLS. The BCCI had that idea at one point but nothing came of it. Are they leaving money on the table?Simpson: In many ways, yes. It comes back to international reach and the way people consume media in India. There is not enough aggregated data on fans: who is watching, how much they spend, where they watch and when they watch. That information is important for streaming platforms and advertisers.Indian cricket needs a clear data and digital strategy. It should also look at international markets, where sports consumption models are more mature.For example, an IPL Pass that allows fans in Australia or the Caribbean to watch a limited number of matches each year could attract considerable interest. There is an opportunity to build more direct relationships with fans and generate revenue that is currently being missed.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.body: India's search for the next generation of fast-bowling stars ahead of the 2027 ODI World Cup appears to have found an exciting prospect in Gurnoor Brar. Hopefully, as he plays more games and gets more experience, he'll become more consistent with his line and length. He's got the pace, he's got the bounce. articles.body: NEW DELHI: New Zealand captain Mitchell Santner admitted that batting was difficult during the second ODI against India, praising both teams' bowlers for making the most of the challenging conditions.India secured a four-wicket victory through the DLS method after rain interrupted the match, taking a 2-0 lead in the five-match series.Unlike the previous ODI, where India comfortably chased down the target of 143 runs with Virat Kohli scoring a brilliant 74, the second match saw both batting line-ups struggle.New Zealand were bowled out for just 134 runs, while India's chase also became difficult as the visiting bowlers kept picking up wickets.Speaking after the match, Santner explained that the pitch offered plenty of assistance to fast bowlers and felt his team could have managed a better total despite the difficult conditions."It was one of those wickets where the seamers looked pretty challenging on. I know Axar bowled quite nicely, but the Indian quicks were in and around it as well, and they all bowled pretty well. [Lessons from the match] As a batting unit, we know it was going to be a tricky surface. But even if there was a potential way of scraping to 160 or 180, we could have gone from there. But yeah, I think they bowled well as well, and obviously, with the weather around, it is always going to be a bit tough to start, and they exploited it very well."Santner praises bowlers from both sidesThe New Zealand skipper also appreciated his team's bowling effort, particularly the way they continued taking wickets and prevented India from getting an easy win. Jacob Duffy and Kyle Jamieson picked up three wickets each, putting the hosts under considerable pressure during the chase.Santner said his bowlers understood that taking early wickets was important and did a good job of keeping India on the back foot."It was a tricky wicket. There is no hiding it. I think they (India) bowled really well, especially at the top, challenged us, and obviously, wickets at the start are never ideal. But I think we were still probably a little bit under at the halfway stage, knowing that there was still a little bit in it, which was nice. And the boys bowled really well," he remarked.Speaking about the bowling performance, he added, "Like we said at Eden Park, it would have been easy for us to just go out there and expect things to happen. But we bowled really well. We started well, and I guess the only way to get into that target was to take wickets at the top. We managed to do that, and then I think the guys coming back in, spell after spell, managed to get the breakthroughs throughout, which is key in ODI cricket."India's Gurnoor Brar was the standout bowler, finishing with figures of 4/30. Auqib Nabi and Anshul Kamboj also claimed two wickets each as New Zealand were dismissed for 134 in 41 overs. Daryl Mitchell top-scored with 55, while Santner contributed 31.Santner provides update on Blair TicknerDuring the match, New Zealand pacer Blair Tickner suffered a blow to his helmet while batting and was replaced by Matthew Fisher as a concussion substitute. Santner provided an update on his teammate, saying the team was waiting to see how he recovered."He is back at the hotel, so hopefully he pulls up okay. But yeah, he has had a concussion recently, so it is one of those ones you want to give it some time."In reply, India were reduced to 47/4 after early dismissals of Shubman Gill, Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli. Shreyas Iyer scored 30, while KL Rahul remained unbeaten on 26 to keep the chase alive. India reached 113/7 before rain stopped play. With the DLS par score at 109, India secured a four-wicket win and strengthened their position in the series.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Towhid Hridoy's 242* creates history as Bangladesh batter shatters all-time Test record against West Indies
articles.summary: Towhid Hridoy produced a knock for the ages, smashing an unbeaten 242 to script history for Bangladesh and pull his side back from the brink in the second
articles.body: Towhid Hridoy produced a knock for the ages, smashing an unbeaten 242 to script history for Bangladesh and pull his side back from the brink in the second Test against West Indies in Sylhet. In an innings that combined extraordinary resilience with breathtaking power-hitting, Hridoy registered the highest individual score by a Bangladesh batter in Test cricket, transforming a potential first-innings collapse into a 30-run lead.Bangladesh were staring at a substantial deficit after slipping to 184 for 7 shortly before Lunch on the third day. But Hridoy refused to surrender, orchestrating a stunning lower-order revival that saw the hosts add 202 runs with their final three wickets to reach 386.Hridoy enters Bangladesh's record books with monumental 242Hridoy became only the fourth Bangladesh batter to register a Test double-century, joining an elite list featuring Mushfiqur Rahim, Tamim Iqbal and Shakib Al Hasan. His unbeaten 242 also eclipsed Mahmudul Hasan Joy's 171 against Ireland to become the highest individual Test score at the Sylhet venue.The right-hander's innings was equally remarkable for its power-hitting. He smashed 11 sixes, taking him within one of the world record for most sixes in a Test innings, jointly held by Wasim Akram and Yashasvi Jaiswal. He also surpassed Tamim's previous Bangladesh record for most sixes in a single Test innings.From 29 overnight to a record-breaking double-centuryHridoy's transformation on the third day was extraordinary. He resumed on 29 off 80 deliveries but shifted gears dramatically, bringing up his century before Lunch. With wickets falling at the other end, he took responsibility for the scoring and repeatedly put the West Indies bowlers under pressure.Roston Chase bore the brunt of his assault, while Shamar Joseph and Jayden Seales also struggled to contain the batter. Hridoy brought up his 150 with a wristy flick off Joseph before reaching the double-century in the final session with a single off Warrican.Lower-order partnership turns the tide for BangladeshTaijul Islam played a crucial supporting role, adding 22 off 56 balls during a 117-run eighth-wicket partnership with Hridoy. His ability to occupy the crease allowed Hridoy to dictate the tempo and keep the scoreboard moving.Even after Taijul's dismissal, Hridoy continued his assault alongside Taskin Ahmed. The latter provided valuable support before falling to Seales, bringing Bangladesh's innings to a close at 386. Hridoy remained unbeaten on 242 after facing down the West Indies attack and carrying his side to a first-innings lead.Brief scores: West Indies 356 and 7/0 trail Bangladesh 386 (Towhid Hridoy 242*, Mushfiqur Rahim 34; Jomel Warrican 4/104) by 23 runs.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Josh Tongue ruled out of Australia ODIs with toe injury, England suffer fresh pace blow
articles.summary: England have suffered a setback ahead of their three-match ODI series against Australia, with fast bowler Josh Tongue ruled out due to a toe injury.
articles.body: England have suffered a setback ahead of their three-match ODI series against Australia, with fast bowler Josh Tongue ruled out due to a toe injury. The right-arm pacer will return to the United Kingdom for further assessment, leaving England without one of their promising fast-bowling options for the upcoming limited-overs assignment.Tongue, who was not included in England's plans for the five-match T20I series as he prepares for the team's upcoming Test tour of South Africa, has reportedly been carrying a problem with his left big toe since the recent tour of Pakistan. The injury also restricted his participation in the tri-series, where he featured in just one of England's four matches.Josh Tongue's injury concerns continue after Pakistan tourThe 28-year-old's latest setback comes after an interrupted run in Pakistan, where the toe problem limited his involvement. He will now undergo further medical assessment in the UK to determine the extent of the injury and his recovery timeline.A regular feature of England's Test side over the past 12 months, Tongue has emerged as an important part of the country's fast-bowling plans. He made his ODI and T20I debuts earlier this year and has been viewed as one of England's promising pace options alongside Jofra Archer, Gus Atkinson and Sonny Baker.England begin Australia tour with warm-up winEngland have already made a winning start to their tour of Australia, beating their opponents in a 50-over warm-up match in Perth on Saturday. The three-match ODI series is scheduled to begin next Friday, followed by a five-match T20I series.Tongue's absence will be a concern as England look to manage their fast-bowling resources across a demanding winter schedule. With the pacer not part of the limited-overs plans in the first place, the immediate focus will be on assessing his fitness ahead of the upcoming Test commitments.South Africa Test tour next on England's agendaEngland are scheduled to play a three-Test series in South Africa after their assignments in Australia. articles.title: 'He kept it simple': Former India coach Paras Mhambrey decodes Mohammed Shami's success
articles.summary: Former India bowling coach Paras Mhambrey reflects on what made Mohammed Shami one of India’s greatest fast bowlers.
articles.body: Former India bowling coach Paras Mhambrey reflects on what made Mohammed Shami one of India’s greatest fast bowlers.Excerpts:Q: You worked closely with Mohammed Shami for several years. What, in your view, was his greatest skill as a fast bowler?Paras Mhambrey: A couple of things stand out. First and foremost was his seam presentation. Very few bowlers in world cricket have had that kind of upright seam position. As a batter, you never quite knew whether the ball would come in or go away after pitching. He kept asking questions of you every delivery. I’ve seen very few bowlers who could do it as consistently as Shami. S Sreesanth was one. After that, Shami stands out. The other thing was his simplicity. He wasn’t overly data-driven or information-heavy. He kept things very simple. He knew exactly what he wanted from a session and what he needed to do to prepare for a game. That clarity really stood out.Q: Was he one of the more self-sufficient bowlers you worked with? Did he require very little technical intervention?Mhambrey: At that level, most established fast bowlers have already figured out their technique. The technical work is usually done when they’re younger and still developing. With Shami, as with most senior bowlers, our conversations were more tactical than technical. He had a fair idea about batters and game plans. Sometimes it was just about discussing a couple of finer points or reinforcing something he already knew. The role of a coach was often to put certain thoughts in front of him and let him process them. He was very experienced and very aware of his own game.Q: What was unique about the way Shami trained and prepared?Mhambrey: He was never a gym-first cricketer. In fact, if memory serves me right, I hardly ever saw him spending long hours in the gym. Of course, he worked on fitness, but he was primarily skill-driven. For him, the most important thing was bowling. He would bowl a lot because he understood that was what sharpened his skill, gave him confidence and improved his control.He belonged more to the old-school generation of fast bowlers who believed that if you wanted to become a better bowler, you had to bowl more. I think that’s one of the biggest reasons for his success.Q: Why was he so effective in India, where conditions generally favour spin bowlers?Mhambrey: He surprised people with his pace. He was much quicker than many batters realised.He wasn’t someone who sprinted into the crease, but he had excellent rhythm and could reproduce that rhythm ball after ball. Batters often underestimated his speed through the air.That’s why you saw so many bowled and lbw dismissals. By the time batters adjusted to the pace of the wicket or the bowler, he had already hurried them into making a mistake.He wasn’t a 150 kmph bowler, but he was definitely quicker than people gave him credit for.Q: He earned the tag of ‘Second-Innings Shami’. What made him even more dangerous as a match progressed?Mhambrey: Accuracy. His ability to hit the same length and the same channel over and over again.Add to that the seam position. As a batter, you could see the seam standing upright but still didn’t know whether the ball would come in or go away. That uncertainty is what made him so dangerous.That’s why he picked up so many bowled and lbw wickets throughout his career.Q: Were you surprised he didn’t get another opportunity in Test cricket after returning to domestic cricket and performing well?Mhambrey: Personally, I would have loved to see him represent India again, in Test cricket and in other formats as well. He’s played Ranji Trophy cricket, he’s done well and, honestly, he’s simply a joy to watch. Sometimes you sit in the dressing room and watch him bowl and he makes everything look so easy.Having said that, we’re not privy to the conversations he may have had with the selectors or the team management. There may have been discussions we don’t know about. Shami would know that better than anybody else. But as someone who has watched him closely, I would certainly have loved to see him play more Test cricket.Q: Any training-ground memory that captures his competitiveness?Mhambrey: I remember one session at the NCA after he had returned from rehab. We were practising on the Chinnaswamy side wickets in Bengaluru. I don’t remember who the batter was, but what struck me was the pace and bounce he generated almost effortlessly. He wasn’t even running at full tilt, yet the batter was clearly uncomfortable.When you watch him from close quarters, you realise how quick he is off the wicket. The seam movement, the bounce, the pace: it was unbelievable. That session reminded me why batters hated facing him in the nets.Q: Has cricket become too reliant on fitness metrics and not enough on actual bowling workloads and performances?Mhambrey: Every generation is different, but if you look at Shami, Jasprit Bumrah, Bhuvneshwar Kumar, Ishant Sharma or Umesh Yadav, they all bowled a lot. That generation developed skill through workload. Fitness was important, but it was a supplement to bowling, not a substitute for it. If you want control, you need to bowl. If you want to know your limits and understand your body, you need to bowl. That’s how you discover your threshold and learn how much extra effort you can produce when the team needs it.These bowlers knew their bodies because they had put in the work over many years. Ishant played more than 100 Tests not because he bowled a few overs in the nets. He bowled thousands of overs over the course of his career. That’s the lesson for young fast bowlers. Skill remains the primary requirement. The more you bowl, the better you understand your craft, your body and your game.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Late release, upright seam, heavy ball: Decoding Mohammed Shami's sorcery
articles.summary: Few bowlers possessed the ability to strip a batter of his technique, judgement, and ego like Mohammed Shami.
articles.body: Few bowlers possessed the ability to strip a batter of his technique, judgement, and ego like Mohammed Shami. The fast bowler from a nondescript village in Uttar Pradesh’s Sahaspur, which literally translates to the “land of courage”, bowled with a big heart, indefatigable spirit, and unmatched skill over 64 Tests.Former England captain Alastair Cook’s dismissal during the Visakhapatnam Test in 2016 was a case in point. Shami bowled a series of outswingers that forced Cook to play away from his body. On cue, he then delivered a perfect inswinger that jagged back sharply to sneak past Cook's defence and cannon onto the stumps.“It’s all in those beautiful wrists,” Shami’s childhood coach Badruddin Siddiqui told TOI.“The reason for his success was that he released the ball late and did not rush through his action. This helped him extract late swing off the track. With those malleable wrists, he made subtle changes at the point of release that batters found hard to pick,” the coach demystified Shami’s skill set. Like S Sreesanth, Shami possessed one of the most upright, God-gifted seam positions in world cricket. Shami was also a bit of a paradox because of the ability to make the old ball skid low while also hurling the ‘heavy ball’ that flew past the batter’s nose. The ‘heavy ball’ — the delivery that pitches shorter and reaches the batter quicker than expected, and hits the bat with extra force despite bowling from a relatively smooth, upright run-up — became Shami’s calling card on numerous overseas tours. The 2018 Johannesburg Test was a classic example: he dismantled South Africa, cruising at 124/1, for 177 to hand India a landmark 63-run win. Shami finished with figures of 5/28, unleashing his trademark ‘heavy ball’ on the spicy Wanderers pitch. At times, he could be erratic even when the conditions were loaded in his favour. But without any warning, he would return with a magical, match-altering spell against the run of play. This streak of unpredictability made Shami irresistible, and it was instrumental in India winning more matches abroad, especially under Virat Kohli’s captaincy. Shami was also a great senior, who passed on his art and tricks of the trade to youngsters.“I learnt a lot of things from him during my time in the IPL. Subtle things like bowling at the death and with the semi-new ball,” Uttar Pradesh pacer Ankit Rajput said.At 36, Shami had been performing admirably in this Ranji season, picking up 14 wickets in his last three games. Yet, the constant snubs and time away from international cricket had hurt him.“He was trying hard to make a comeback. But after a point, he realised he was not going to get another chance in Tests, which is why he chose to retire,” Badruddin explained.“He wants to play the ODI World Cup next year. He has kept that window open,” he added. Shami is India’s highest wicket-taker in the 50-over World Cups, with 55 scalps from 18 games at an impressive average of 13.5.The sorcerer of seam signs off from Tests, leaving a gaping hole in India’s bowling roster. Finding Shami’s replacement would be as difficult as locating Sahaspur on the India map.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.summary: Rohit Sharma etched his name in ODI history on Saturday as he became the batter with the most sixes against New Zealand in the 50-over format.
articles.body: Rohit Sharma etched his name in ODI history on Saturday as he became the batter with the most sixes against New Zealand in the 50-over format. The India opener achieved the milestone during the second ODI at Hnry Stadium in Wellington, moving past former Pakistan all-rounder Shahid Afridi's long-standing record.Rohit needed two sixes to surpass Afridi's tally of 50 maximums against the Black Caps and reached the landmark during his 23-run knock off 28 deliveries in India's chase of 135. The 39-year-old brought up the record with two sixes off New Zealand pacer Kyle Jamieson, one each in the seventh and ninth overs.The Mumbai batter, who had registered a six-ball duck in the series opener in Auckland on Wednesday, bounced back with a couple of maximums to take his tally to 51 sixes in 34 innings across 36 ODIs against New Zealand.Afridi had struck 50 sixes in 35 innings from 38 matches against the Black Caps between 1996 and 2015. West Indies great Chris Gayle occupies the third spot with 45 sixes, while former Sri Lanka opener Sanath Jayasuriya is fourth with 41. articles.body: Former India cricketer Dodda Ganesh has questioned India's decision to use Axar Patel at No. 5 in overseas conditions, arguing that the all-rounder should not be considered a long-term option at that batting position. He also felt the team management's approach was coming at the expense of KL Rahul's opportunity to spend more time at the crease.Reacting to India's batting order during the second ODI against New Zealand in Wellington, Ganesh took to X to express his reservations about Axar's suitability for the role, particularly in SENA countries (South Africa, England, New Zealand and Australia)."I say it again: Axar Patel can’t be your no 5 in SENA countries. He could play a cameo here and there but he’s definitely not a long term solution. You are denying KL Rahul the game time #NZvIND," Ganesh wrote.The former cricketer's comments come amid India's continued experimentation with their middle-order combinations. The team has often pushed Rahul down to No. 6 to maintain a left-right batting combination, with Axar getting an opportunity higher up the order.That strategy came under scrutiny during the rain-affected second ODI, where India's batting line-up struggled against New Zealand's disciplined pace attack while chasing a target of 135.After the visitors' bowlers had bundled out New Zealand for 134, India found themselves in early trouble on a surface offering bounce and movement. Jacob Duffy struck twice, dismissing captain Shubman Gill for a first-ball duck and Virat Kohli for seven, while Rohit Sharma managed 23 off 28 deliveries before departing.Axar, promoted to No. 5, could contribute only seven runs before falling while attempting a ramp shot. Shreyas Iyer made 30 off 46 balls but failed to convert his start, leaving India under pressure at 47/4.Rahul, meanwhile, provided the stability India desperately needed. Initially cautious, he negotiated the challenging conditions before shifting gears with a couple of pull shots, including a six. He remained unbeaten on 26 as India reached 113/7 in 26 overs when rain brought the contest to an end.India were four runs ahead of the DLS par score at that stage, securing a four-wicket victory and taking a 2-0 lead in the five-match series.The bowling effort had laid the foundation for the win, with Gurnoor Brar claiming career-best figures of 4/30. Auqib Nabi picked up 2/31, while Anshul Kamboj returned 2/25. New Zealand were eventually dismissed for 134 in 41 overs, with Daryl Mitchell top-scoring with 55.Ganesh's remarks have once again brought the spotlight on India's middle-order strategy and whether Rahul should be given a higher batting position instead of being pushed down to accommodate the left-right combination.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Slippery turf, testing conditions: KL Rahul keeps his cool as India take 2-0 series lead against New Zealand
articles.summary: It has been a while since bowlers dominated a white-ball series quite so emphatically, putting batters under pressure and dictating terms.
articles.body: It has been a while since bowlers dominated a white-ball series quite so emphatically, putting batters under pressure and dictating terms. In an era of 350-plus totals and 300-run chases, these low-scoring contests have been a refreshing reminder that tight bowling, rather than brute-force batting, can make for compelling cricket.India’s star-studded batting lineup was blown away by New Zealand’s pacers before a composed KL Rahul produced a vital, unbeaten 26 off 38 balls, including two sixes and two fours, to guide the visitors to a hard-fought four-run win via the DLS method in a rain-affected second ODI in Wellington on Thursday. Rahul, aided by vice-captain Shreyas Iyer’s 30 off 46 balls and veteran opener Rohit Sharma’s 23 off 28, made sure India’s young fast bowlers were rewarded for their excellent work. Gurnoor Brar was the standout, returning career-best figures of four for 30 in his 10 overs.India now lead the five-match series 2-0 and will have a chance to seal it in the third ODI in Hamilton on Tuesday. Chasing 135 in 47 overs, they were in trouble at 113 for seven after 26 overs, still needing 22 with three wickets in hand, when rain returned. With the DLS par score at 109 at that point, India edged home.Brar was India’s standout performer, using his height to extract steep bounce and operating with raw pace and aggression. He removed Tom Latham (7), Glenn Phillips (0), Mitchell Santner (31) and Nathan Smith (3). The tall Punjab pacer found strong support from Auqib Nabi, who took two for 31 in seven overs, and Anshul Kamboj, who returned two for 25 in eight. The three seamers shared eight wickets as India bowled New Zealand out for 134 in 41 overs, making full use of the pace, bounce and movement on offer.India were never going to find the chase easy on such a surface, but the task proved tougher than expected. Skipper Shubman Gill fell for a rare first-ball duck, caught at second slip by Henry Nicholls off Jacob Duffy in the second over. Duffy struck again when Virat Kohli drove uppishly to short cover, leaving India 17/2.Rohit lived dangerously after being dropped by Nathan Smith at deep backward square leg, but briefly counterattacked with his trademark pull shots, hitting Kyle Jamieson for two sixes. Axar Patel, promoted to No. 5, struggled for timing before ramping Matthew Fisher to deep backward point for 7 off 17 balls, leaving India 47 for four in the 13th over.Shreyas played a few attractive strokes but once again fell to the short ball, with Jamieson dismissing him for 30. At 86 for five, India were in trouble before Rahul steadied the innings. He produced some of the shots of the match, pulling Smith for a four and a six in the 16th over before dispatching Jamieson for another six in the 23rd. India lost Naman Dhir (12) and Kamboj (1) late, but Rahul’s calm presence kept them ahead of the DLS mark.Earlier, playing his third ODI, Nabi claimed his maiden international wicket when Tim Seifert was caught by Kamboj at mid-wicket for a duck. He then removed Will Young (11), who edged a fine delivery to Rahul. Kamboj had Nicholls playing on before Brar struck twice in the 20th over, dismissing Latham and Phillips with short-pitched deliveries.Axar also impressed, taking 2/28 in nine overs, including the key wicket of Daryl Mitchell, who made a fighting 55 off 104 balls.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘There was nothing wrong’: Sunil Gavaskar shuts down criticism of Gautam Gambhir's decision to bat Axar Patel at No. 5
articles.summary: Legendary India batter Sunil Gavaskar has backed the team management's decision to promote Axar Patel ahead of KL Rahul in the second ODI against New
articles.body: Legendary India batter Sunil Gavaskar has backed the team management's decision to promote Axar Patel ahead of KL Rahul in the second ODI against New Zealand, explaining the tactical thinking behind the move despite the all-rounder's failure with the bat.India were chasing a modest target of 135 at Hnry Stadium in Wellington but found themselves in early trouble against New Zealand's disciplined pace attack. After losing Shubman Gill, Virat Kohli and Rohit Sharma, the visitors slipped to 39/3. Axar was then sent in at No. 5, ahead of Rahul, but could manage only seven runs before falling, leaving India struggling at 47/4.The decision by head coach Gautam Gambhir and captain Gill to push Axar up the order attracted criticism from sections of fans and experts. However, Gavaskar felt there was sound reasoning behind the move, particularly the advantage of disrupting a bowling attack's plans by introducing a left-handed batter."The bowlers have slight difficulty if a left-handed batter comes because you have to change the line and length you would have for a right-hander. In trying to do that, your line can change slightly even to the right-hander, where more chances of getting runs are created," Gavaskar explained, speaking on Sony Sports network after the game.The former India captain also pointed out that such tactical decisions should not be judged solely by their outcome, as they can produce different results on different occasions."There was nothing wrong with that thought process. If Axar had scored runs, you would have said how good the captaincy was. Such moves work at times and don't work on other occasions, and it didn't work this time. You also knew there was a solid player like Rahul after him. That's why you experiment at times," he added.Axar's promotion was not an entirely unfamiliar move for India. The left-hander has previously been trusted with a higher batting position in important matches, most notably during the 2024 T20 World Cup final, when he forged a crucial partnership with Virat Kohli.He also occupied the No. 5 position ahead of Rahul throughout India's victorious Champions Trophy 2025 campaign.In Wellington, however, it was Rahul who eventually took responsibility for keeping India's chase on track. After walking in following Axar's dismissal, he combined with Shreyas Iyer, who contributed 30 off 46 deliveries, to steady the innings.Rahul was cautious initially, playing 18 dot balls in his first 20 deliveries before finding opportunities to accelerate. He remained unbeaten on 26 when rain stopped play, with India at 113/7 after 26 overs.India were four runs ahead of the DLS par score of 109 when the match was abandoned, handing the visitors a four-wicket victory and a 2-0 lead in the five-match series.The win was set up by an impressive performance from India's young pace attack. Gurnoor Brar claimed career-best figures of 4/30, while Auqib Nabi and Anshul Kamboj picked up two wickets apiece to dismiss New Zealand for 134 in 41 overs.Daryl Mitchell top-scored for the hosts with 55, but New Zealand's total proved insufficient as India secured another DLS victory in the series.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.body: Gurnoor Brar produced a memorable performance with the ball in the second ODI against New Zealand, registering the second-best bowling figures by an Indian fast bowler in ODIs in New Zealand. The young pacer returned figures of 4/30 at Hnry Stadium in Wellington, joining an elite list headed by former India speedster Javagal Srinath.Brar's impressive spell helped India bundle out New Zealand for just 134 in 41 overs in the rain-affected contest on Saturday. His effort placed him behind Srinath's 4/23, recorded in Auckland in 2003, in the list of best ODI bowling figures by an Indian pacer on New Zealand soil.The 29-year-old used his pace and bounce effectively to trouble the New Zealand batting line-up, particularly through the middle overs. After Auqib Nabi and Anshul Kamboj made early inroads, Brar took charge with a double-wicket maiden, dismissing Tom Latham and Glenn Phillips off successive short-pitched deliveries.Latham was forced to reach for a wide bouncer and offered a catch, while Phillips was caught off a delivery directed towards his body. Both wickets left New Zealand reeling at 53/5.Brar continued to trouble the hosts with his aggressive approach, finishing with career-best figures of 4/30. Nabi supported him with 2/31 from seven overs, while Kamboj picked up 2/25 in eight overs. Arshdeep Singh also maintained pressure with an economical spell of 0/16 in seven overs.New Zealand's innings had begun to unravel in the opening powerplay itself. Nabi removed Tim Seifert for a duck, while Kamboj accounted for Will Young and Henry Nicholls as the hosts slumped to 29/3.Daryl Mitchell offered some resistance with a patient 55 off 104 deliveries, adding 59 runs with captain Mitchell Santner, who made 31 off 38 balls. However, the partnership was not enough to prevent New Zealand from being bowled out for a modest total.Best ODI bowling figures by an Indian pacer in New ZealandFiguresBowlerVenueYear4/23Javagal SrinathAuckland20034/30Gurnoor BrarWellington20264/52Javagal SrinathNapier19954/55Mohammed ShamiNapier20144/70Arshdeep SinghAuckland2026India's bowlers sent down 176 dot balls during New Zealand's innings, laying the foundation for another victory in the series.However, the visitors had to work hard in the chase after New Zealand's pacers exploited the movement and bounce on offer. Jacob Duffy dismissed Shubman Gill for a first-ball duck and Virat Kohli for seven, while Rohit Sharma contributed 23 before departing.Axar Patel managed only seven, and Shreyas Iyer's 30 provided some resistance before he was dismissed. With India struggling at 47/4, KL Rahul and Iyer attempted to rebuild the innings.Rahul remained unbeaten on 26 when rain interrupted play at 113/7 after 26 overs. articles.title: Retired Hurt: Mohammed Shami deserved a better farewell
articles.summary: As tributes poured in from former players, fans and the BCCI after Mohammed Shami announced his retirement from Test cricket on Friday, they all pointed
articles.body: As tributes poured in from former players, fans and the BCCI after Mohammed Shami announced his retirement from Test cricket on Friday, they all pointed to the same truth: India had bid farewell to one of its finest pacers.Over 13 years, Shami played 64 Tests, claimed 229 wickets and helped transform India’s pace-bowling identity. Amid the praise, though, lingered uncomfortable questions: Was he valued enough in the final phase of his career?Like several senior Indian cricketers before him, Shami’s Test journey ended not on a cricket field but through a social media post. There was no farewell Test among passionate fans in a full stadium. For a bowler who had such a massive impact on India’s fortunes, the ending felt understated and incomplete.Former India coach Ravi Shastri voiced that sentiment forcefully. “Without him, the fast-bowling unit would not have functioned,” Shastri said on Sony Sports Network during the second ODI in Wellington on Saturday.The former coach was convinced Shami still had plenty left to offer. “I definitely thought he had another 30-40 wickets left in him. He should have played in the last 12 months and should have played Tests here.”Former India bowling coach Paras Mhambrey shared a similar view.“Personally, I would have loved to see him represent India again, in Test cricket and in other formats as well,” Mhambrey told TOI. “He’s played Ranji Trophy and Duleep Trophy, done well and, honestly, he’s a joy to watch. He makes everything look so easy.”Mhambrey stopped short of questioning the decision-makers, though, acknowledging that outsiders were unaware of the conversations that may have taken place between Shami, the selectors and the team management.Shastri’s strongest criticism, however, was reserved for the repeated doubts over Shami’s fitness despite his performances for Bengal in domestic cricket.“He was bowling 15 to 20 overs daily. What else do you want a player to do to prove his fitness?” Shastri asked.Shami’s final Test came in the World Test Championship final against Australia at The Oval in June 2023. For a bowler who continued to play domestic cricket thereafter, it felt like a forced full stop.Ask Mhambrey what made Shami special and the answer arrives quickly.“Very few bowlers in world cricket had that kind of upright seam presentation. As a batter, you never knew whether the ball would come in or go away. He kept asking questions every ball.”That seam position became Shami’s trademark. Few bowlers of his generation attacked the stumps as relentlessly. Of his 229 Test wickets, 101 came through bowled or lbw dismissals.Mhambrey believes another underrated aspect of Shami’s success was his simplicity.“He wasn’t data-driven. He kept things very simple. He knew what he wanted and how he wanted to prepare. There wasn’t too much noise around his process.”The numbers underline just how valuable he was. On spin-friendly home surfaces, where fast bowlers often played supporting roles, Shami remained a match-winner. He claimed 76 wickets in India at an extraordinary average of 22, and India did not lose any of the 21 home Tests in which he featured.Part of that success stemmed from a quality often overlooked.“He surprised people with his pace,” Mhambrey said. “He was much quicker than batters felt. He had great rhythm and could replicate it again and again. That’s why you saw so many bowled and lbw dismissals.”Few teammates enjoyed facing him in the nets. Dinesh Karthik once described the experience as “torture”, while Shami’s fierce practice battles with Virat Kohli could have been part of many highlight reels.For Shami, bowling was never a chore. It was romance.During the Covid lockdown, he returned to his farmhouse in Amroha, built clay practice tracks and spent hours bowling and running to stay sharp. That old-school philosophy, Mhambrey believes, defined an entire generation of Indian fast bowlers.“Shami, Bumrah, Ishant, Umesh, Bhuvneshwar, they bowled a lot. Skill came first. Fitness supplemented that skill. If you want control, you need to bowl. If you want to know your limits, you need to bowl.”Perhaps that is why Shami earned the label “Second-Innings Shami”, a bowler whose threat often intensified as matches wore on. Mhambrey observes that his pace rarely dipped, his accuracy remained relentless and his upright seam challenged both edges of quality batters.Which makes it all the more ironic that he was never afforded a second innings in his own Test career.“In this 13-year journey, this cap and this ball made me Mohammed Shami,” he said in his farewell message. “I did fall, I did get hurt, I did get injured. But I stood up again for this badge.”For that, Shami deserved one final opportunity to walk away on his own terms, but he probably retired hurt.BEST OF MOHAMMED SHAMIMohammed Shami’s rare blend of pace, seam movement and relentless accuracy made him a match-winner. Diptayan Hazra revisits five of his finest Test spells...5-47 vs West Indies, Kolkata, 2013: Shami announced himself in style on Test debut. On a sluggish Eden surface, the he generated sharp movement with the old ball and attacked the stumps, finishing with 5-47 in the second innings and match figures of 9-118. Six of his wickets were bowled and one LBW, offering an early glimpse of his trademark dismissal patterns.6-56 vs Australia, Perth, 2018: On one of the fastest pitches in world cricket, Shami produced the best figures of his Test career. With Australia looking to set up the match in the second innings, he struck at regular intervals, using pace and seam movement to claim 6-56. It’s the only six-wicket haul by an Indian bowler in a Test in Perth.5-28 vs South Africa, Wanderers, 2018: Defending 241 on a lively Wanderers surface, India seemed to be losing when South Africa raced to 124-1. Enter Shami. The pacer ripped through the middle and lower order with a devastating spell of 5-28 to turn the match.5-44 vs South Africa, Pretoria, 2021: Shami spearheaded India’s attack in the opening Test, claiming 5-44 as South Africa were bowled out for 197. His effort helped India secure a crucial first innings lead of 130, setting the platform for a landmark victory. He claimed three more in the second innings.5-35 vs South Africa, Vizag, 2019: Proof that Shami could be just as lethal on Indian pitches. After going wicketless in the first innings, he roared back with a superb 5-35 in the second, removing some key batters including skipper Faf du Plessis and Temba Bavuma.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: How the Kolkata maidans shaped UP-born Mohammed Shami
articles.summary: KOLKATA: Growing up in a small village in Uttar Pradesh’s Amroha district, where life revolved around sugarcane fields and mustard farms, Mohammed Shami’s
articles.body: KOLKATA: Growing up in a small village in Uttar Pradesh’s Amroha district, where life revolved around sugarcane fields and mustard farms, Mohammed Shami’s rise to international cricket seemed improbable. Yet the son of a farmer somehow defied the odds to become one of India’s greatest fast bowlers.Fast bowling ran in the family. Shami’s elder brother, Haseeb, was known locally for his pace before injuries curtailed his career. Determined to give his son a chance, father Tousif Ahmed sent Shami to train under coach Badruddin Siddique in Moradabad, 22 km from their village of Sahaspur, Alinagar.The road was far from smooth. Shami failed to make Uttar Pradesh age-group teams for three successive years before an unexpected opportunity changed everything.A Kolkata club approached Siddique looking for a fast bowler and the coach immediately recommended his most promising pupil. Within days, a 16-year-old Shami boarded the Punjab Mail to Kolkata.Playing for Dalhousie Athletic Club in the Maidan circuit for Rs 500 a match, Shami soon caught the eye of Town Club official Debabrata Das, who signed him for Rs 70,000 a season and accommodated him at his home.ALSO READ: Retired Hurt: Mohammed Shami deserved a better farewellUnlike many modern cricketers, Shami had little interest in gyms or weight training. He preferred running and long bowling spells. His fondness for biryani became legendary in Kolkata’s club circuit, with officials jokingly motivating him with promises of a plate after a match-winning spell.Breaking into Bengal’s senior side remained difficult until then chief selector Sambaran Banerjee spotted him in a local match against Eastern Railway.“I watched him from beside the sightscreen. He took four wickets bowling with the wind. I asked the captain to bring him on against the wind and he took two more. I knew immediately this boy could spearhead India’s attack one day,” Banerjee recalled.What impressed him most was a trait that would later become Shami’s hallmark.“His seam position and release point were exceptional. That very evening I pushed for his inclusion in the Bengal squad.”Shami repaid that faith by claiming three wickets on his Ranji Trophy debut against Assam at Eden Gardens in 2010. Former Bengal captain Manoj Tiwary remembers being struck by his smooth action and natural pace. “He was a lambi race ka ghoda,” Tiwary said.He also points out the influence Wasim Akram had when the Pakistan great joined Kolkata Knight Riders as bowling coach. “Shami wasn’t a regular in the XI initially, but I saw how Akram worked on his game,” Tiwary recalled.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘I haven’t thrown anyone under the bus’: Usman Khawaja hits back amid Sandpapergate row
articles.summary: The Sandpapergate scandal that rocked Australian cricket in 2018 has returned to the spotlight following fresh revelations from Usman Khawaja, who has
articles.body: The Sandpapergate scandal that rocked Australian cricket in 2018 has returned to the spotlight following fresh revelations from Usman Khawaja, who has claimed that the entire team was aware of the ball-tampering attempts during the Test series against South Africa.Excerpts from Khawaja's upcoming autobiography, Sabr, published by the Sydney Morning Herald (SMH) on Saturday, suggested that the controversial practice was not restricted to the third Test in Cape Town but had also been attempted in the preceding match. The revelations have triggered strong reactions, with former Australia coach Darren Lehmann rejecting Khawaja's claims and ex-England captain Michael Vaughan also expressing his displeasure.Amid the growing controversy, Khawaja took to social media on Sunday to clarify his comments, insisting that his account had been misrepresented and that he stood by what he had written.“Alright, it’s time to clear up some facts because the media has taken this to the moon, as expected.“I stayed quiet yesterday, but number one, if you read my article, you would have seen when I mentioned it was all of us that’s implying that, whether we like it or not, we are all responsible for what happened. Together, as a team, we need to take that collectively. That is all,” the former Australian batter said.However, Khawaja stopped short of retracting his assertion that the players knew about the ball-tampering episode.“But now that everyone’s talking, am I going to deny that everyone knew? Nah. I won’t deny that either.“But I never speak on behalf of anyone else in my book. Contrary to all the headlines the clickbait media would have you think. Don’t get caught up in this s***.”The former opener also addressed suggestions that he had chosen to make the revelations eight years after the incident to generate publicity and boost sales of his autobiography. Khawaja maintained that he had deliberately held back the account until the Australian team had returned from South Africa."What I say now isn’t a reflection of them anymore, and now my words don’t influence the team at all. I speak for myself.“But even so, I refused to publish any of this while the boys were still in South Africa. That’s why I called Pat (Cummins).“Why would someone who really wants to increase the sale of his book refuse the greatest marketing opportunity he has? I haven’t thrown anyone under the bus... those three guys [Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft] who took the blame for all of us, they’re the victims,” he said.Khawaja reveals two teammates opposed collective responsibilityFurther details from the autobiography, reported by Code Sports, have also shed light on a disagreement within the Australian dressing room after the Cape Town Test. Khawaja claimed that two members of the team objected to his proposal that the players collectively accept responsibility for what had happened.“This was the most disappointing thing for me. I knew who those two guys were, and it was ludicrous; out of everyone, it was them. It showed me their true colours, though. When the going got tough, all they cared about was themselves. But I was not going to stop fighting this cause,” Khawaja wrote.The issue resurfaced years later when Cameron Bancroft appeared to suggest in an interview that Australia's bowlers had knowledge of the ball-tampering operation.Following those remarks, Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc and Nathan Lyon issued a joint statement distancing themselves from the incident.Khawaja's autobiography further claims that he contacted then head coach Justin Langer and CEO Todd Greenberg after Bancroft's interview. He reportedly urged them to ensure that the entire team accepted responsibility rather than placing the burden solely on the bowling group.According to Khawaja, both Langer and Greenberg agreed with his suggestion. However, the eventual statement released publicly came only from the four Australian bowlers, leaving the former batter disappointed with how the matter was handled.The latest revelations have reopened questions surrounding one of the darkest episodes in Australian cricket, with Khawaja maintaining that responsibility for the incident extended beyond the three players who were formally punished.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘Wrong to eliminate toss in U-23 matches’: Dilip Vengsarkar urges BCCI to restore it
articles.summary: MUMBAI: Former India captain Dilip Vengsarkar has criticised the BCCI’s decision to scrap the toss in the Col CK Nayudu Trophy for the past two seasons,
articles.body: MUMBAI: Former India captain Dilip Vengsarkar has criticised the BCCI’s decision to scrap the toss in the Col CK Nayudu Trophy for the past two seasons, urging the board to restore the practice from next season. In May 2024, then BCCI secretary Jay Shah announced that the toss would be done away with in the men’s under-23 tournament for the 2024-25 season, with the visiting team given the choice of batting or bowling first.The move was aimed at curbing the practice of home teams preparing spin-friendly pitches to gain an advantage. The BCCI’s move was the first instance of the toss being scrapped in Indian domestic cricket. The England and Wales Cricket Board had also done away with it in the County Championship from 2016 to 2019, before restoring it in 2020.“It’s absolutely wrong to do away with the toss in U-23 matches. The element of toss brings a different charm and excitement to a cricket match,” Vengsarkar told TOI.Vengsarkar said that teams must learn to adapt to different conditions. “The wicket and conditions are the same for both teams. If you play a balanced team, you can cope with any conditions. And what happens if you make a wicket to suit your strength, but lose the toss? A toss adds a different, but necessary dimension to a cricket game,” he said.“Sometimes, when you are not sure about whether to bat or bowl first, it could be a good toss to lose. The BCCI should reintroduce the toss in its U-23 tournament from the next season. There’s no question about it,” he added.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
